approachQuestion.prompt:
An unissued serial

The read-only random-access array `issued` lists distinct positive integers in strictly increasing order. In the infinite sequence 1,2,3,..., remove every listed integer. Return the kth remaining integer, counting from one.

Constraints: 1 <= n <= 200000; 1 <= issued[i] <= 10^9; 1 <= k <= 10^9. Use signed 64-bit arithmetic. Prefer a method whose worst-case work grows least with n and the numeric values, then least working memory.

Examples: issued=[2,3,7,11], k=5 -> 8 (the first five remaining values are 1,4,5,6,8); issued=[1,2,3], k=2 -> 5; issued=[6], k=2 -> 2.
constraints: The requested value can lie before the first listed integer or after the last.
The array contains only issued integers, not every integer up to its maximum.

options.text: Find the first index i with issued[i]-(i+1)>=k by iterative lower-bound search, using n as the absent-boundary sentinel. Return k+i.
options.feedback: At index i, issued[i]-(i+1) counts missing positive integers through issued[i]. These counts never decrease. The first boundary says exactly i listed values precede the answer, including i=n when it lies beyond all entries.

options.text: Find the same boundary recursively by copying the retained half at each step, carrying its original index offset, then return k plus that original boundary index.
options.feedback: Original offsets keep the missing-count calculation correct, but copied slices and recursive frames add avoidable work and space. Search the supplied array with indices instead.

options.text: Starting at 1, enumerate integers and advance a pointer through issued, counting unlisted values until k are found.
options.feedback: This is correct but can enumerate a billion or more integers despite a tiny input. It ignores the rank calculation available from a probe.
This assumes every earlier positive integer was issued. For issued=[6], k=2 the result should be 2, whereas this returns 8.

feedback.reason: At index i subtract i+1 from the issued value to count missing positives through that point. Search for the first count reaching k. If its index is i, exactly i issued integers shift the kth missing value, so return k+i. If no count reaches k, use i=n.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only gap-boundary: an iterative lower-bound search computing issued[mid]-(mid+1) directly, followed by returning k+lo. Let n be the array length. Signed 64-bit arithmetic and random access are constant time. No arrays are copied and no recursion or hashing is used. Choose the tightest pair.
constraints: Use worst-case bounds. Count all working memory including any stack; exclude supplied inputs and the scalar result.

options.text: O(n + k) time, O(1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Compute missing rank per midpoint and halve the index search interval.
details: The missing count at a midpoint is one subtraction, so each halving costs constant time. Searching n indices takes O(log(n+1)) time; computing k+i afterward is constant. No array proportional to k or n is allocated.
“O(log(n + 1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Missing counts are computed at probes, with scalar search bounds.
“O(log(n + 1)) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: Missing-rank computation uses the probed value and index directly; no n-entry missing-value table is built.
“O(n + k) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Search is over issued indices, not every positive integer through the missing answer.
“O(1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The first missing-rank threshold may require logarithmically many index probes.

methodReveal.title: Search the missing-count boundary
methodReveal.description: At index i subtract i+1 from the issued value to count missing positives through that point. Search for the first count reaching k. If its index is i, exactly i issued integers shift the kth missing value, so return k+i. If no count reaches k, use i=n.
